subject: Cloud Computing
title: The Uber 2016 Cover-Up
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Uber 2016 Cover-Up usable.

hook.text: Hackers stole 57 million Uber user records in 2016. Uber's response: pay the hackers $100,000 and hide the breach.

buildup.text: The attackers found AWS credentials in a GitHub repository. With those keys, they accessed Uber's S3 data.

discovery.text: Uber paid the hackers through its bug bounty program, disguising the ransom as a legitimate security payout.

twist.text: The cover-up lasted a year. When it was exposed, the CSO was fired and later criminally charged for obstruction.

climax.text: The lesson: breaches happen. Cover-ups destroy companies. Transparency and rapid response are the only acceptable path.

punchline.text: The breach was bad. The cover-up was worse.

quiz.question: How did attackers initially access Uber's cloud data?
options: They found AWS credentials in a public GitHub repository
They guessed the CEO's password after 10 attempts
Uber accidentally made all S3 buckets publicly accessible

details.summary: In 2016, Uber suffered a breach exposing 57 million user and driver records after attackers found AWS credentials in a GitHub repository. Instead of disclosing the breach, Uber paid the attackers $100,000 and concealed the incident for over a year.
details.whyItMatters: Uber's cover-up demonstrated that hiding breaches creates far more damage than disclosure. It led to legal consequences and became a case study in how not to handle security incidents.
takeaways: AWS credentials were exposed in a public GitHub repository
57 million records were stolen via those credentials
The cover-up led to legal action and reputational damage

faq.question: How did the attackers access Uber's data?
faq.answer: Uber engineers had accidentally committed AWS access keys to a private GitHub repository. Attackers found the keys, used them to access Uber's S3 buckets containing rider and driver data, and then extorted Uber for payment to delete the stolen data.

faq.question: What were the consequences of the cover-up?
faq.answer: Uber paid $148 million in a settlement with state attorneys general. The CISO was convicted of obstruction. The incident became a landmark case establishing that concealing breaches carries severe legal and financial consequences beyond the breach itself.
